meta.subtitle: Pharma programs drive growth and gross margin, but at 28.8x consensus forward earnings the shares already sit near fair value

analystCommentary:
Paysign's 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 shows a business in the middle of a mix transition: patient affordability revenue from pharma clients now exceeds plasma donor compensation revenue. Management raised its FY26 outlook to $114.0M to $117.0M in revenue, and both plasma utilization and pharma program counts moved the right way in Q2'26.

We rate the shares HOLD. The business is executing, but the stock has already re-rated and trades near the top of its $3.08–$14.93 52-week range. Our scenarios leave almost no expected upside from here, against a Bear case that needs only slower growth and a lower multiple rather than any break in the business.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Paysign, Inc. is a vertically integrated provider of prepaid card products and processing services, headquartered in Henderson, Nevada. It acts as both payment processor and prepaid card program manager, so it earns revenue across the card lifecycle: cardholder fees, interchange, card program management fees, transaction claims processing fees, software license fees, breakage and settlement income. Its cards are sponsored by issuing bank partners.

Two client groups drive the business. Pharmaceutical companies use its patient affordability programs to fund copay assistance, and blood and plasma collection organizations use its cards to pay donors. It also sells life science software to plasma collectors under the Apherion brand.

The company reports a single reportable segment. FY25 revenue was $82M, up 40.5%.

thesis.body: Our HOLD rests on the gap between operating momentum and price. Pharma patient affordability is compounding and has carried gross margin higher, though the company does not guide to further gross margin gains (see Financials). Plasma has steadied on a per-center basis even as the center count shrinks. The FY26E consensus of ~$114.7M sits inside the raised revenue outlook, toward its low end. At 28.8x forward earnings, a multiple that rests on consensus EPS, the shares need delivery above the guide to move higher.

catalysts: Q3'26 results against the company's revenue guide and its active-program exit target, the next test of the raised outlook.
Pace of new pharma patient affordability program launches, the main driver of growth and mix.
Evidence that the plasma center count has stopped falling.
Deployment of a growing unrestricted cash balance, including the existing repurchase authorization.
risks: Valuation: a growth miss would test the forward multiple the shares now carry.
Plasma attrition: customers closing centers or selling them to operators that use another provider.
Policy: changes to rules on copay accumulator or maximizer programs could hit the pharma business.
Earnings quality: part of Q2'26 profit came from a one-time earn-out adjustment and a low tax rate.
Dilution: a planned request to expand the 2023 Equity Incentive Plan.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Q2'26 revenue rose 48.1% to $28.3M. Gross margin improved to 63.3% from 61.6% in Q2'25, and the company attributes the gain to a greater mix of pharma revenue. Cost of revenues rose 41.4%, slower than revenue, even with a new customer service contact center that went live in November 2025.

Operating margin reached 24.8%, up from 7.5% a year earlier, and most of that step came from operating expenses rather than gross margin. Total operating expenses rose 5.5%, or 15.1% excluding a one-time, non-cash $990,000 benefit from a fair value adjustment on contingent consideration tied to the Gamma acquisition, far slower than revenue. Excluding that benefit, operating margin was 21.3%. The release credits both mix shift and expense discipline for the margin expansion, and on these figures expense discipline did more of the work.

The reading that cuts the other way is the outlook. The company guides Q3'26 gross margin to 61.0% to 63.0% and FY26 gross margin to 62.0% to 63.0%, at or below the Q2'26 level, so it is not guiding to further mix-driven gross margin gains. Future margin progress therefore has to come from operating leverage.

Net income was $6.76 million, or $0.11 per fully diluted share, against $0.02 in Q2'25. The effective tax rate was 14.5% against 32.1% a year earlier, and the company ties the difference to discrete items linked to its higher stock price. We therefore treat part of the earnings step-up as non-recurring. Adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, rose 113.0% to $9.61 million.

On an annual view, operating margin expanded to 9.0% in FY25 from 1.7% in FY24, and stands at 17.0% on a trailing-twelve-month basis.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Paysign exited Q2'26 with $27.37 million of unrestricted cash and zero bank debt, according to the August 5, 2026 earnings release. Vendor data shows FY25 total debt of $8M; the two measures differ in scope, and we use the company's zero bank debt figure when assessing leverage.

Restricted cash rose to $149.11 million. Those funds back customer card funding and pharmaceutical claim reimbursements and carry a matching offset in current liabilities. That structure explains a current ratio of 1.14 on a TTM basis: the ratio reflects pass-through client funds rather than a liquidity squeeze.

Management states in the 10-Q that cash on hand, excluding restricted cash, together with its forecast for revenues and cash flows, will sustain operations for the next twenty-four months. The company also says it can fund expansion into new verticals from internally generated funds if it does not raise capital.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
FY25 free cash flow was $51.2M, a 62.5% FCF margin, against a 38.6% margin in FY24 and FY25 net income of $7.6M. Capital expenditure was -$1.2M in FY25, so the platform is not capital intensive.

The counter-case to discounting that cash flow is its consistency: the FCF margin has been high in every year of the five-year series, including 50.6% in FY21, 66.3% in FY22 and 57.9% in FY23. Over the same years operating margin stayed in the single digits and was negative in FY21 and FY23. Cash conversion that far above operating profit, year after year, points to the balance sheet rather than the income statement. The client funds described in the balance sheet discussion pass through the company, so operating cash flow can move with program funding that belongs to clients.

The figures we have do not separate those flows from earnings. We therefore value the shares on earnings and read the 9.2% TTM FCF yield as an upper bound on cash earnings power rather than a measure of it.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The shares trade at 54.3x trailing earnings, 29.1x EV/EBITDA and 7.9x sales. On forward estimates the P/E falls to 28.8x NTM and ~22.9x FY27E. The NTM multiple rests on consensus EPS.

The consensus and company figures disagree for FY26. Consensus FY26E EPS of $0.49 sits above the company's diluted EPS outlook of $0.35 to $0.37, and the two are not on a stated common basis. On the company's outlook, the forward multiple would be materially higher. We use consensus throughout the valuation, including FY27E EPS of $0.62, because it is the basis that runs past FY26, and we note that this choice flatters the multiple.

All five covering analysts rate the stock Buy, yet the consensus target of $14.10 is essentially the current price, with a $15.00 median and an $11.50–$15.00 range.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Pharma program launches run ahead of the 165 to 170 Q3'26 exit target, FY26 revenue lands above the $117.0M top of the outlook, and the market holds the current forward multiple as FY27E earnings come into view.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Paysign delivers inside its FY26 outlook and tracks consensus FY27E revenue of $133.7M and EPS of $0.62, and the shares hold close to the ~22.9x FY27E multiple, so the price moves little from here.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Plasma center losses continue, pharma launches slip or copay accumulator rules tighten, and growth falls below the Q3'26 guide; the multiple de-rates toward that of a slower-growth processor.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight Base at 50% and Bull and Bear at 25% each. The Base carries twice the weight of either tail because the company has just raised its outlook, consensus revenue sits inside that outlook, and the Q3'26 guide gives near-term visibility; each tail needs results to break from that guide in one direction. The weighted values are $4.50 for Bull, $7.25 for Base and $2.50 for Bear, for a probability-weighted fair value of $14.25.

That is an expected upside of +1.0% against a Bear-case downside of -29.1%, a reward/risk of 0.03x. Our caution rests on that pairing: the scenario set offers almost no expected return for a real chance of a large loss. The Bear requires no break in the business, only slower growth and a lower multiple.

Our target range brackets the Base and reflects a stock that we think is fairly priced for delivery within guidance.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body:
The August 5, 2026 earnings release splits Q2'26 revenue by industry.

Pharma revenue {+ rose 88.9% +} to $14.65 million, driven by 51 net patient affordability programs launched over the past 12 months and higher management, setup and claims processing fees. Plasma revenue {+ rose 21.4% +} to $13.04 million on more donations and more dollars loaded to cards.

Pharma revenue now exceeds plasma revenue. Plasma still accounts for close to half of quarterly revenue and depends on a center base that is shrinking.

moatFactors.name: Embedded pharma programs
moatFactors.body: Patient affordability programs run on Paysign's claims processing, business rules and contact center, which makes switching a program mid-life costly for a pharma client. The company exited Q2'26 with 148 active programs, and fees scale with claims volume. The counter-case is that each program is a separate sale, and the 10-K warns competitors may offer similar products and force price competition.

moatFactors.name: Plasma center relationships
moatFactors.body: Average monthly revenue per center {+ rose to $7,699 +} versus $7,098, which the release describes as stronger utilization at existing centers. We read that as part of the plasma recovery covered under Growth, not as evidence of advantage. The center count {- fell to 561 from 607 -}, partly because a customer sold centers to a company that uses another provider. Center-level relationships therefore move with the ownership of the center, which caps this factor's durability.

moatFactors.name: Integrated platform
moatFactors.body: Paysign manages the full prepaid lifecycle in-house, from card design and production to a 24/7/365 bilingual customer service operation. That end-to-end scope is harder to replicate than a single processing layer. It still relies on issuing bank partners to sponsor its cards.

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NARROW. Pharma programs carry the switching costs described above, and they are the core of the rating. Plasma is weaker: the recent utilization gain tracks the market, and the center sale shows those relationships follow the owner of the center. The 10-K frames the industry as one where competitors may match the offering and push pricing down, and the pharma franchise also carries the policy exposure set out under Risks. We would upgrade the rating on evidence of multi-year program retention, which the company does not disclose in the materials we reviewed.

points: **Q3'26 outlook.** The company guides Q3'26 revenue to $28.5M to $30.0M, or 32.0% to 38.9% growth, below the 48.1% Q2'26 rate. The release gives no reason for the step-down.

**Pharma pipeline.** Paysign expects to exit Q3'26 with 165 to 170 active patient affordability programs, up from 148 at the end of Q2'26. Processed claims {+ increased by approximately 54% +} in Q2'26, roughly in line with growth in the program count.

**Plasma normalization.** The 10-Q states the plasma market appears to have returned to normalized growth following elevated plasma inventory levels through much of 2025. The company expects 561 to 563 centers at the end of Q3'26, which would end the decline in the count.
**Volume indicators.** Gross dollar load volume rose 24.3% and gross spend volume rose 24.2% in Q2'26; management names dollars loaded on cards as a primary indicator of revenue.

**Profit outlook.** FY26 guidance calls for Adjusted EBITDA of $35.0M to $38.0M and net income of $21.5M to $23.0M. The Q3'26 guide is the sequential read: Adjusted EBITDA of $9.5M to $10.0M against $9.61 million in Q2'26, and net income of $5.7M to $6.0M against $6.76 million, a quarter that included the $990,000 benefit and a 14.5% tax rate. Profit is guided flat to lower quarter on quarter.

**Optionality.** Paysign earns licensing, hosting and professional service fees from its Apherion software, and the 10-Q names the United States and Mexico as principal target markets for processing services. The company does not size either opportunity.

management.leadership: Mark Newcomer is President and CEO, and Jeff Baker is Chief Financial Officer, per the August 5, 2026 earnings release. In that release, Baker said revenue, operating margin and net income all finished above the high end of guidance, and the company raised its full-year outlook. Beating and raising in the same quarter supports guidance credibility. The counterpoint is that the profit beat leaned on the one-time items discussed under Financials, and the materials we reviewed carry no earlier history of guidance against results, so the evidence is one quarter deep.
management.capitalAllocation: For the rest of 2026, the company plans to keep investing in technology, sales and marketing, cybersecurity, fraud, customer service and regulatory compliance. It evaluates raising capital from time to time to enter new verticals. Share repurchases were -$375,786.00 in FY25, and the 10-Q says the stock repurchase program will remain available over a 36-month period expiring May 7, 2029. Stock compensation expense {- rose 31.2% -} to $1.25 million in Q2'26, and the company intends to seek stockholder approval for more shares under the 2023 Equity Incentive Plan at its next annual meeting, expected on or before June 30, 2027. The proxy reported 55,185,394 shares outstanding as of March 19, 2026, against ~56.46M as of October 2, 2026, a vendor figure derived from market capitalization, so repurchases have not held the share count flat.
management.governance: Our governance view rests on the proxy statement filed March 26, 2026. It reports no related-person transactions and states that all transactions with officers, directors, principal stockholders and their affiliates require Board approval under the company's written Code of Ethics. The Board selected Baker Tilly US, LLP as independent auditor for FY26. The proxy excerpt we reviewed does not cover board composition, director independence or executive pay, so we make no claim on those points. We note that the beneficial ownership of Michael Ngo includes 1,000,000 shares owned by Gamma Innovation LLC, while the company carries contingent consideration from its Gamma acquisition; the proxy does not link the two, and we draw no conclusion beyond flagging earn-out disclosures for monitoring.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 19, 2026, per the proxy, all officers and directors as a group (11 people) beneficially owned 24.5% of the common stock. Mark R. Newcomer held 9,025,728 shares, or 16.3%, including options in a family member's name. That bloc gives insiders real weight in votes such as the planned request to expand the 2023 Equity Incentive Plan, a plan whose awards go in part to the same officers and directors, so outside holders should not read a passing vote as an independent endorsement. The counter-case on alignment is composition: 2,175,001 of the group's shares are options exercisable or grants vesting within 60 days, and Daniel R. Henry's 2.6% is mostly exercisable options. Topline Capital Partners, LP reported 9.7% based on a Schedule 13G filed February 10, 2025; that holding is dated and may have changed.

idiosyncratic: **Copay assistance policy.** The August 5, 2026 release lists potential restrictions on copay accumulator or maximizer programs among its risk factors. The company markets its solutions as mitigating the effects of accumulators and maximizers, so a rule change could reduce the need for the product itself rather than shift it to a rival. Watch: net program additions against the Q3'26 exit target.

**Plasma customer movement.** The release flags the risk that plasma center customers switch to competing providers or close centers; the center sale discussed under the moat shows how that happens. Watch: the center count at the end of Q3'26 against guidance.

**Bank and deposit exposure.** Paysign's cards are sponsored by issuing bank partners, and the 10-Q notes that if a financial institution holding its deposits were placed into receivership, the company may be unable to access that cash. Watch: any change in bank relationships.

**Data security.** The FY25 10-K warns that a breach at Paysign, its issuing banks or service providers could bring litigation, network fines and reputational damage that reduce card use. The exposure grows as load volume rises and more cardholder data passes through the platform. Watch: any incident disclosed by Paysign or an issuing bank partner, and whether the cybersecurity spending planned for 2026 continues.

**Gamma integration.** The release cites integration risk from the Gamma acquisition, and Gamma already moves reported results: Q2'26 operating expenses included the $990,000 fair value adjustment on the earn-out liability, and H1'26 cash flow included payments of other liabilities associated with the acquisition. Further earn-out adjustments would make reported margins harder to read, and the 10-K separately cautions the company may have internal control deficiencies. Watch: contingent consideration adjustments and Gamma-related payments in Q3'26.
risks.systemic: Regulation of the payments industry has increased, per the FY25 10-K, and changes to card association rules or anti-money laundering requirements can raise compliance costs or force product changes. The release notes that an economic downturn could reduce the customer base and demand for the company's products. Both client verticals depend on healthcare spending patterns, plasma collection volumes and pharmaceutical pricing practices that Paysign does not control.

body: We rate Paysign HOLD with a target range of $13 to $16 and a probability-weighted fair value of $14.25.

We would move to BUY on a pullback that opens a wider gap to our Base value without a change in the operating trend, or on Q3'26 results that put program launches above the exit target with the plasma center count stable. We would move lower on a miss against the Q3'26 revenue guide or on policy action against copay accumulator programs.
